verses.text: “You also, son of man, take a tile, and lay it before yourself, and portray on it a city, even Jerusalem.
Lay siege against it, build forts against it, and cast up a mound against it. Also set camps against it and plant battering rams against it all around.

Take for yourself an iron pan, and set it for a wall of iron between you and the city: and set your face toward it. It shall be besieged, and you shall lay siege against it. This shall be a sign to the house of Israel.
“Moreover lie on your left side, and lay the iniquity of the house of Israel on it. According to the number of the days that you shall lie on it, you shall bear their iniquity.
For I have appointed the years of their iniquity to be to you a number of days, even three hundred ninety days: so you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Israel.
“Again, when you have accomplished these, you shall lie on your right side, and shall bear the iniquity of the house of Judah. I have appointed forty days, each day for a year, to you.
You shall set your face toward the siege of Jerusalem, with your arm uncovered; and you shall prophesy against it.
Behold, I put ropes on you, and you shall not turn yourself from one side to the other, until you have accomplished the days of your siege.

“Take for yourself also wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt, and put them in one vessel. Make bread of it. According to the number of the days that you shall lie on your side, even three hundred ninety days, you shall eat of it.
Your food which you shall eat shall be by weight, twenty shekels  a day. From time to time you shall eat it.
You shall drink water by measure, the sixth part of a hin. From time to time you shall drink.
You shall eat it as barley cakes, and you shall bake it in their sight with dung that comes out of man.”
Yahweh said, “Even thus shall the children of Israel eat their bread unclean, among the nations where I will drive them.”

Then I said, “Ah Lord Yahweh! Behold, my soul has not been polluted; for from my youth up even until now I have not eaten of that which dies of itself, or is torn of animals; neither came there abominable meat into my mouth!”
Then he said to me, “Behold, I have given you cow’s dung for man’s dung, and you shall prepare your bread on it.”
Moreover he said to me, “Son of man, behold, I will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem. They will eat bread by weight, and with fearfulness; and they shall drink water by measure, and in dismay;
that they may lack bread and water, be dismayed one with another, and pine away in their iniquity.

footnotes.content: A tile. A piece of clay brick, and on it the holy city sketched—Jerusalem as a map, as a stage. The prophet becomes a sign-bearer, holding up what God sees: not glory anymore, but a siege approaching. Sometimes the plainest acts speak loudest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forts, mounds, rams—the language of war. Ezekiel's hands build a portrait of ruin with siege towers. He speaks through clay what Israel will soon feel in stone and fire. God makes His prophet an instrument of hard truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An iron pan as a wall of iron between prophet and city—a barrier, a boundary. Ezekiel faces Jerusalem across that cold divide, arms raised. This is covenant language inverted: the wall that once kept enemies out now separates God's messenger from His own wayward people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lie on your left side, and bear their iniquity—the weight of a nation's unfaithfulness becomes the burden of one man's body. His posture becomes a parable. There is something about lying still under the weight of others' sin that speaks of intercession, of standing in the gap.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three hundred ninety days—a year for each day, the math of judgment mapped onto flesh. God doesn't hide the cost of bearing witness to His people's fall. The prophet's body becomes a calendar of mercy refused, of grace deferred.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the right side—forty days more for Judah alone. The house divided carries separate weights. Each kingdom, each rebellion, each turning away has its own measure. Yet God counts it all; He knows the shape and sum of every straying.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Set your face toward the siege with your arm uncovered—exposed, vulnerable, prophesying against Jerusalem. There is a tenderness in an uncovered arm, almost childlike. Yet the man must stand and speak hard things against the city he loves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ropes bound me, so I could not turn. The prophet is held fast—not by chains of iron, but by the rope of God's purpose. He cannot flee, cannot flinch, cannot look away. Faithfulness sometimes feels like captivity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, spelt—a harvest gathered into one vessel. Six grains mixed together, ground coarse. It speaks of scarcity, of making do, of the thin bread of exile. The prophet's meal becomes Jerusalem's future meal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty shekels a day, rationed, measured out. Not abundance, not feast-bread, but survival bread—enough, barely, if you count it twice. This is the diet of siege, the diet of judgment. Mercy even here: a number assigned, so death won't be random.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Water by measure, a sixth of a hin—less than a quart for a day. The throat learns thirst. Rationing teaches dependence; measured mercy teaches humility. Even God's judgment carries His strange care—a portion, not destruction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bake it with dung—the bread of the unclean, of the defiled. A hard word, made harder by its plainness. Yet I hear in it a question: what will you not endure to find your way home? What will break you, and what will bend you toward repentance?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The children of Israel shall eat their bread unclean among the nations. Exile is not just distance from home; it is estrangement from the law, from clean worship, from the way you know yourself. Yet even there, God sees; even there, He counts the broken bread.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ah, Lord Yahweh! My soul has not been polluted—Ezekiel cries out in anguish. Even this faithful man draws a line. His protest is not rebellion, but the deep faithfulness of one who has kept the law and now faces a harder obedience. The Lord hears the prayer of those who argue with love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I have given you cow's dung for man's dung—a small mercy, a concession. Not a reprieve, but a lessening. God bends a little toward the conscience of His servant. In judgment there is still room for such grace—not enough to undo the sign, but enough to say: I hear you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem—bread as the staff of life, and God Himself will snap it. The famine is not chance; it is covenant consequence. Yet even here I hear a Father's voice: not anger alone, but the firmness of one who loves enough to let His child feel the cost of walking away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They may lack bread and water, be dismayed one with another, pine away in their iniquity. Readers today hear an echo in these words—not of siege, but of the soul's thirst in exile from God's presence. We know now, in hindsight, that famine was not the worst hunger the people faced. The deepest lack was Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
